doc.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Music at home and long practice hours
summary: His father made a cigar-box ukulele; Carter alone pursued music and practiced for hours with his father's work ethic.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: And how did music play in the home in your childhood?

Well again, everyone seemed to have a talent to play something. I'm the only one who decided to try to make a living at this foolishness. My father made a ukulele out of a cigar box and a stick of wood and some rubber bands and tried to do that. In general I was the only one who spent the time to try to develop, as it turns out, this talent.
I read that you spent as much as eight hours a day practicing in your childhood.

Well, you know, my father instilled a good work ethic in this. While he didn't have to insist that I practiced those kind of hours, it just seemed to me, the only way you get better is by putting in the time. When you have all those siblings; the chores were split up evenly and it was a pretty good time. There wasn't, of course, the distractions that we call them today available. There was very limited television. There weren't the conveniences that you have: the iPod and all those modern devices. No computers. So it was actually easier to focus because there weren't too many things to make focus not possible.
